1. The animation shows how US consumer prices (CPI-U) have eroded purchasing power through annual raises. It compares annual raise rates of 2%, 3%, 3.1% and 6.38% against how often historical stretches of time were at least that high. Each rate has a bar, and the labels say "raise a year" and "all stretches."

2. Bars are added one at a time. First the 2% bar appears with 2.4%. Then the 3% bar appears with 42.4%. Then the 3.1% bar appears and is labeled "half." Last, a 6.38% bar labeled "all · Carl's stretch" appears. A note in frame 4 says "a median of the past, not an expectation." In frames 5 and 6 an "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag appears.

3. As I read the chart, the higher the yearly raise, the larger the share of historical stretches it covers. A 2% raise only kept up with prices in about 2.4% of stretches. A 3% raise kept up in about 42.4%. A raise of about 3.1% kept up in about half. A raise of 6.38% covers all stretches, which is the "Carl's stretch" example. The labels say this is US history only, not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might infer that a payout that rises by a fixed amount, such as 2% a year, may not keep up with price increases. That inference is the viewer's own, and the animation warns against treating the past as a prediction.

5. The animation did not suggest this advice. It is my own conclusion, and the animation only presents the historical comparison with disclaimers.
